# Human-identified examples

Writing that people (editors, award juries, style-guide authors, researchers) singled out as good or bad. Entries marked *described* paraphrase a text too long or too restricted to quote.

## X01 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (boohoo) (2021)

- **Before:** increase the share of wallet opportunity through a new capital light and low risk operating model
- **After:** Sell more to existing customers with a cheap, low-risk setup. (Paraphrase of the Campaign's translation.)
- **Why:** Jargon stacked into noun phrases; no actor, no concrete action.
- **Rules:** WORD-07, WORD-01
- **Source:** https://plainenglish.co.uk/golden-bull-award-winners-2021

## X02 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (NHS England) (2021)

- **Before:** provider collaboratives will be a key component in enabling ICSs to deliver their core purpose
- **After:** Groups of healthcare providers working together will help local health systems do their main job. (Paraphrase of the Campaign's translation.)
- **Why:** Undefined acronym, abstract jargon ('key component', 'deliver their core purpose').
- **Rules:** WORD-07, CLR-08
- **Source:** https://plainenglish.co.uk/golden-bull-award-winners-2021

## X03 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Pensions Dashboards Programme) (2021)

- **Before:** With our procurement of the principal digital architecture underway
- **After:** We have started buying the main computer system.
- **Why:** Nominalization ('procurement') and inflated words hide a simple action.
- **Rules:** ACT-02, CLR-07
- **Source:** https://plainenglish.co.uk/golden-bull-award-winners-2021

## X04 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (SP Energy Networks) (2021)

- **Before:** EREC G59 requirements must be implemented by generation owners
- **After:** If you own a generator, you must update its protection equipment by 1 September 2022.
- **Why:** Undefined codes; passive voice hides who must act.
- **Rules:** CLR-08, ACT-03
- **Source:** https://plainenglish.co.uk/golden-bull-award-winners-2021

## X05 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (jungle.com) (2003)

- **Before:** We are currently in the process of consolidating our product range
- **After:** We're selling fewer products.
- **Why:** Filler ('currently in the process of') and euphemism.
- **Rules:** FILL-07
- **Source:** https://worldwidewords.org/pec2003.html

## X06 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Lloyds pharmacy) (2003)

- **Before:** The cognitive process that staff will go through when interpreting prescriptions
- **After:** Our pharmacists read prescriptions quickly because they know the drugs well.
- **Why:** Abstract, inflated phrasing for a simple claim.
- **Rules:** WORD-02, CLR-06
- **Source:** https://worldwidewords.org/pec2003.html

## X07 Bad: Center for Plain Language, Grand WonderMark (Charles Schwab) (2013)

- **Before:** (Magazine ad in which judges estimated nearly 90% of the language was legalese.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Asked for trust while making it impossible to tell what the firm would do with the reader's money.
- **Rules:** CLR-07, WORD-07
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/center-for-plain-language-honors-march-of-dimes-with-the-grand-clearmark-award-charles-schwab-captures-the-grand-wondermark-award/

## X08 Bad: Center for Plain Language, WonderMark (Department of Homeland Security) (2013)

- **Before:** (Deferred-action form whose opening paragraph held an 81-word sentence.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Bureaucratic density; a judge said it barely read as English.
- **Rules:** ORD-02, CLR-14
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/center-for-plain-language-honors-march-of-dimes-with-the-grand-clearmark-award-charles-schwab-captures-the-grand-wondermark-award/

## X09 Bad: Center for Plain Language, WonderMark (1&1 Internet) (2013)

- **Before:** (Webhosting upgrade letter full of technical terms, sent to non-programmer customers.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Wrong audience: a submitter with a law degree couldn't follow it.
- **Rules:** CLR-01, CLR-08
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/center-for-plain-language-honors-march-of-dimes-with-the-grand-clearmark-award-charles-schwab-captures-the-grand-wondermark-award/

## X10 Bad: Denis Dutton, Bad Writing Contest, first prize (Judith Butler, in diacritics) (1998)

- **Before:** (A one-sentence passage of academic theory built from chains of abstract nouns.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Run by the journal Philosophy and Literature to expose scholarship it called pretentious gibberish. Butler defended the passage in the New York Times.
- **Rules:** ACT-02, ORD-02, CLR-09
- **Source:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Dutton

## X11 Bad: Helen Sword, 'Zombie Nouns,' New York Times (2012)

- **Before:** The proliferation of nominalizations in a discursive formation ...
- **After:** Writers who overload their sentences with abstract nouns tend to sound pompous. (Paraphrase of Sword's rewrite.)
- **Why:** Seven nominalizations, no human actor, no action. Sword built it as a deliberate bad example.
- **Rules:** ACT-02, ACT-01
- **Source:** https://yale-nus.edu.sg/academics/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2021/12/Nominalizations-Are-Zombie-Nouns-The-New-York-Times.pdf

## X12 Bad: Steven Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014)

- **Before:** (A psychology-journal sentence about 'stimulus' and 'poststimulus events.') *(described)*
- **After:** Tap someone's wrist, elbow, and shoulder in quick succession, and they feel one tap hopping up the arm.
- **Why:** Curse of knowledge: technical abstraction where a concrete description was available.
- **Rules:** CLR-09, CLR-06
- **Source:** https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/the-curse-of-knowledge-pinker-describes-a-key-cause-of-bad-writing

## X13 Before / after: George Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946)

- **Before:** (Orwell's parody: Ecclesiastes 9:11 rewritten as abstract 'modern English' about success, failure, and unpredictable factors.) *(described)*
- **After:** I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
- **Why:** The King James original (public domain) is concrete and visual; the parody replaces every image with abstraction.
- **Rules:** CLR-06, CLR-07
- **Source:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_and_the_English_Language

## X14 Before / after: SEC, A Plain English Handbook (1998)

- **Before:** We made an application ...
- **After:** We applied ...
- **Why:** Nominalization with a weak verb.
- **Rules:** ACT-02
- **Source:** https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf

## X15 Before / after: SEC, A Plain English Handbook (1998)

- **Before:** We will have no stock ownership of the company.
- **After:** We will not own the company's stock.
- **Why:** Hidden verb ('ownership').
- **Rules:** ACT-02
- **Source:** https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf

## X16 Before / after: SEC, A Plain English Handbook (1998)

- **Before:** The following summary is intended only to highlight certain information contained elsewhere in this Prospectus.
- **After:** This summary highlights some information from this Prospectus.
- **Why:** Superfluous words.
- **Rules:** FILL-07
- **Source:** https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf

## X17 Before / after: SEC, A Plain English Handbook (1998)

- **Before:** Persons other than the primary beneficiary may not receive these dividends.
- **After:** Only the primary beneficiary may receive these dividends.
- **Why:** Negative turned positive.
- **Rules:** CLR-05
- **Source:** https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf

## X18 Before / after: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

- **Before:** The following information must be included in the application for it to be considered complete.
- **After:** You must include the following information in your application.
- **Why:** Passive to active; addresses the reader as 'you'.
- **Rules:** ACT-03, CLR-01
- **Source:** https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing

## X19 Before / after: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

- **Before:** We conduct an analysis of the data.
- **After:** We analyze data.
- **Why:** Hidden verb.
- **Rules:** ACT-02
- **Source:** https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing

## X20 Before / after: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

- **Before:** These sections describe types of information that would satisfy the application requirements of Circular A-110 as it would apply to this grant program.
- **After:** These sections tell you how to meet the requirements of Circular A-110 for this grant program.
- **Why:** Conditional tense and abstraction replaced with present tense and 'you'.
- **Rules:** CLR-10, CLR-01
- **Source:** https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing

## X21 Before / after: GOV.UK clear-language guidance (2024)

- **Before:** An electronic travel authorisation is needed.
- **After:** You need an electronic travel authorisation.
- **Why:** Active voice addressed to the reader.
- **Rules:** ACT-03
- **Source:** https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/

## X22 Before / after: Google developer documentation style guide

- **Before:** Clear it if the cache is full.
- **After:** If the cache is full, clear it.
- **Why:** Condition before instruction.
- **Rules:** CLR-03
- **Source:** https://developers.google.com/style/translation

## X23 Before / after: Google developer documentation style guide

- **Before:** Configuring the rules is required before deploying.
- **After:** You must configure the rules before you deploy.
- **Why:** -ing forms and passive replaced with 'you must'.
- **Rules:** CLR-04, ACT-03
- **Source:** https://developers.google.com/style/translation

## X24 Before / after: Google developer documentation style guide

- **Before:** Only request one token.
- **After:** Request only one token.
- **Why:** Modifier placed next to what it modifies.
- **Rules:** CLR-02
- **Source:** https://developers.google.com/style/translation

## X25 Good: Center for Plain Language, Grand ClearMark (Health Literacy Media & Novartis) (2026)

- **Text:** (Clinical-trial results summary for teens and young adults with diabetes.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Judges praised short sentences, common words, a tone right for young readers without condescension, and regular testing with the audience.
- **Rules:** CLR-07, ORD-02, CLR-01
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/awards/clearmark/2026-clearmark-awards-winners/

## X26 Good: Center for Plain Language, ClearMark (Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation) (2026)

- **Text:** (Patient guide: dietary supplements and myeloma.) *(described)*
- **Why:** A one-sentence 'quick takeaway' at the top, familiar words, short active sentences, basics-to-details order, clear headings.
- **Rules:** ORD-01, CLR-07, ACT-03
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/awards/clearmark/2026-clearmark-awards-winners/

## X27 Good: Center for Plain Language, ClearMark (Maximus) (2026)

- **Text:** (Health-insurance tax form letter and FAQ, Massachusetts Health Connector.) *(described)*
- **Why:** Opening statement of purpose and required action; logically ordered headings; a checklist that anticipates questions.
- **Rules:** ORD-01, CLR-11
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/awards/clearmark/2026-clearmark-awards-winners/

## X28 Good: Center for Plain Language, ClearMark legal category (2013)

- **Text:** (Proposed rule, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.) *(described)*
- **Why:** A regulation that avoids jargon, uses familiar nouns and active verbs, tables, vertical lists, and question-and-answer headings.
- **Rules:** CLR-07, ACT-03, CLR-11
- **Source:** https://centerforplainlanguage.org/center-for-plain-language-honors-march-of-dimes-with-the-grand-clearmark-award-charles-schwab-captures-the-grand-wondermark-award/

## X29 Good: Joseph Kimble, survey of Michigan lawyers (2006)

- **Text:** (Plain-language rewrite of a Michigan judicial opinion.) *(described)*
- **Why:** 61% of 251 lawyers preferred it. Top reasons: less unnecessary detail and an opening summary. Average sentence length fell from 25 to 19 words.
- **Rules:** ORD-01, ORD-02
- **Source:** https://www.michbar.org/file/barjournal/article/documents/pdf4article2972.pdf

## X30 Good: Warren Buffett, preface to the SEC Plain English Handbook (1998)

- **Text:** Write with a specific person in mind.
- **Why:** Buffett pictured his sisters: smart, but not experts in finance.
- **Rules:** CLR-01
- **Source:** https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf

## X31 Bad: A Sun customer, quoted in Morkes & Nielsen's web-writing research (NN/g) (1997)

- **Before:** Sun is exceptionally committed to...
- **After:** Yes, Sun still supports that Solaris version. (Our illustration: answer the question with the fact.)
- **Why:** The customer asked whether Sun would support an older Solaris platform and got self-promotion instead of an answer. They said they wanted fact, not platitudes.
- **Rules:** WORD-10, ORD-01, TPL-06
- **Source:** https://www.nngroup.com/articles/concise-scannable-and-objective-how-to-write-for-the-web/

## X32 Before / after: Plain English Campaign, before-and-after examples

- **Before:** If there are any points on which you require explanation or further particulars we shall be glad to furnish such additional details as may be required by telephone.
- **After:** If you have any questions, please phone.
- **Why:** Twenty-eight words of formal padding reduce to six.
- **Rules:** CLR-07, FILL-07
- **Source:** https://www.plainenglish.co.uk/campaigning/examples/before-and-after

## X33 Before / after: Plain English Campaign, before-and-after examples

- **Before:** High-quality learning environments are a necessary precondition for facilitation and enhancement of the ongoing learning process.
- **After:** Children need good schools if they are to learn properly.
- **Why:** Abstract nouns replaced by the real actors (children) and a concrete noun (schools).
- **Rules:** ACT-02, CLR-06, ACT-01
- **Source:** https://www.plainenglish.co.uk/campaigning/examples/before-and-after

## X34 Before / after: Plain English Campaign, before-and-after examples

- **Before:** (A council's library letter about displaying benefit-rights posters, full of 'provenance and authoritativeness' and 'items of a disputatious or polemic kind'.) *(described)*
- **After:** (The Campaign's version thanks the writer, then says the library needs to see the posters first to check they won't offend anyone.)
- **Why:** The rewrite answers the actual request and states the next step.
- **Rules:** ORD-01, CLR-07
- **Source:** https://www.plainenglish.co.uk/campaigning/examples/before-and-after

## X35 Before / after: Plain English Campaign, before-and-after examples (2010)

- **Before:** (A UK parking ticket: 'must be paid not later than the last day of the period of 28 days beginning with the date on which this PCN was served'.) *(described)*
- **After:** (The Campaign's version: 'You must now pay a penalty charge of £70 within 28 days', with the exact date, and 'Do not pay the traffic warden'.)
- **Why:** Addresses the reader as 'you', gives the actual deadline, spells out the abbreviation, and drops the all-caps shouting.
- **Rules:** CLR-01, CLR-08, FMT-02
- **Source:** https://www.plainenglish.co.uk/campaigning/examples/before-and-after

## X36 Bad: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Halton Borough Council) (2005)

- **Before:** (A 630-word single sentence in a footpath-diversion notice.) *(described)*
- **Why:** One sentence tried to describe an entire route by distances from building corners. A map or numbered steps would do it.
- **Rules:** ORD-02, CLR-11
- **Source:** https://www.plainenglish.co.uk/campaigning/examples/long-sentences

## X37 Before / after: Federal Plain Language Guidelines, 'Write short sentences' (2011)

- **Before:** The proposal is presented to an employer who agrees to negotiate an individualized job that meets the employment needs of the applicant and real business needs of the employer.
- **After:** We prepare a preliminary proposal to present to an employer who agrees to negotiate a job that meets both his and your employment needs.
- **Why:** Passive and third person replaced with 'we' and 'you'; the full rewrite also splits the original into shorter sentences.
- **Rules:** ORD-02, CLR-01, ACT-03
- **Source:** https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/concise/write-short-sentences/

## X38 Before / after: CDC, Simply Put (2010)

- **Before:** Heart disease and lung cancer are caused by smoking.
- **After:** Smoking causes heart disease and lung cancer.
- **Why:** Passive to active.
- **Rules:** ACT-03
- **Source:** https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf

## X39 Before / after: CDC, Simply Put (2010)

- **Before:** Following safety precautions can reduce food-borne disease transmission.
- **After:** Cook meat until it is not pink in the middle.
- **Why:** Vague, passive abstraction replaced by a concrete action.
- **Rules:** CLR-16, CLR-06
- **Source:** https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf

## X40 Before / after: CDC, Simply Put; HHS Health Literacy Online 2.4 (2010)

- **Before:** Do not ride your bicycle without wearing a helmet.
- **After:** Wear your helmet every time you ride your bicycle.
- **Why:** Negative instruction turned positive.
- **Rules:** CLR-05
- **Source:** https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf

## X41 Before / after: CDC, Simply Put (2010)

- **Before:** Seat Belts
- **After:** Wear your seatbelt. It could save your life.
- **Why:** One-word label replaced by a complete-idea heading.
- **Rules:** FMT-04
- **Source:** https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf

## X42 Before / after: CDC, Simply Put (2010)

- **Before:** Feel for lumps about 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter.
- **After:** Feel for lumps about the size of a pea.
- **Why:** A familiar comparison instead of a measurement.
- **Rules:** CLR-17, CLR-06
- **Source:** https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf

## X43 Before / after: HHS, Health Literacy Online 2.6 (2016)

- **Before:** Tests may be needed to find out what's wrong.
- **After:** You may need a test to find out what's wrong.
- **Why:** Passive to active, addressed to the reader.
- **Rules:** ACT-03, CLR-01
- **Source:** https://odphp.health.gov/healthliteracyonline/2016/write/section-2-6/

## X44 Before / after: HHS, Health Literacy Online 2.6 (2016)

- **Before:** Your primary doctor may refer you to a neurologist.
- **After:** ... A neurologist is a doctor who treats problems related to the brain and nervous system.
- **Why:** Defines the term in context, the first time.
- **Rules:** CLR-08
- **Source:** https://odphp.health.gov/healthliteracyonline/2016/write/section-2-6/

## X45 Before / after: HHS, Health Literacy Online 2.3 (2016)

- **Before:** (A definition of blood pressure, then 'get it checked often.') *(described)*
- **After:** Check your blood pressure every 2 years, especially if you are age 40 or older.
- **Why:** States the behavior first, specifically.
- **Rules:** ORD-01, CLR-15, CLR-16
- **Source:** https://odphp.health.gov/healthliteracyonline/2016/write/section-2-3/

## X46 Before / after: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, top 10 tips

- **Before:** You can access Office apps across your devices, and you get online file storage and sharing.
- **After:** Store files online, access them from all your devices, and share them with coworkers.
- **Why:** Starts with verbs; drops 'you can'.
- **Rules:** FILL-07
- **Source:** https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/top-10-tips-style-voice

## X47 Before / after: Microsoft Writing Style Guide

- **Before:** Since you created the table, you can change it.
- **After:** Because you created the table, you can change it.
- **Why:** 'Since' can mean time or cause.
- **Rules:** CLR-21
- **Source:** https://learn.microsoft.com/ko-kr/style-guide/word-choice/use-simple-words-concise-sentences

## X50 Bad: William Zinsser, On Writing Well (a university president's phrase)

- **Before:** very considerable potentially explosive expressions of dissatisfaction
- **After:** (campus protests)
- **Why:** Zinsser's example of clutter: a stack of modifiers around an abstract noun for a concrete event.
- **Rules:** WORD-01, ACT-02, CLR-06
- **Source:** https://www.litcharts.com/lit/on-writing-well/chapter-2-simplicity

## X51 Bad: William Zinsser, On Writing Well, ch. 16

- **Before:** (A school principal's notice about a 'special phone communication system'.) *(described)*
- **After:** (Ask parents to call the teacher.)
- **Why:** Zinsser taught 40 principals four rules: clarity, simplicity, brevity, humanity.
- **Rules:** CLR-07, WORD-02
- **Source:** https://www.litcharts.com/lit/on-writing-well/chapter-16-business-writing-writing-in-your-job

## X52 Before / after: Bryan Garner, LawProse Lesson 287

- **Before:** (A 34-word sentence beginning 'The Internal Revenue Code contains numerous methods...') *(described)*
- **After:** (A 20-word rewrite: 'the tax code', 'many methods', 'IRS errors', 'imposing personal liability on IRS employees isn't among them'.)
- **Why:** Garner estimates a line edit can cut a typical brief or contract by about 25% without changing its meaning.
- **Rules:** FILL-07, CLR-07
- **Source:** https://lawprose.org/lawprose-lesson-287-plague-wordiness/
